entries.note: One of 13 cards offered Nov 7 (data/ideas/cards.json), never chosen or turned down: the straw had already gone first. Not a no.

card.topic: The doctor who rode a rocket to find out what a crash does to you
card.hook: A doctor straps himself to a rocket sled and hits a thousand kilometres an hour, to find out what stops you dying in a crash.
card.people_think: It's the speed that kills you, and nobody could survive stopping that fast.
card.truth: Speed itself does nothing. It's how fast you stop and what you hit, and a body held properly can take far more than anyone believed: he took 46 times the force of gravity.
steps: In the 1940s the limit a body could survive was thought to be about 18 g.
Crash reports showed pilots' seats breaking loose and harnesses failing in fairly mild crashes, so some probably survived the hit and died when the cockpit's fittings gave way.
So he rode a sled on rails into water brakes, going from 1,017 km/h to nothing in about 1.4 seconds.
A harness made his body stop with the seat, so nothing hit anything hard.
He took a peak of 46.2 g and lived, with the blood vessels in his eyes burst and his sight more or less back the next day.
card.turn: He spent the rest of his life pushing for seat belts in cars, and a sensor wired backwards on his project gave Murphy's Law its name.
card.first_picture: A man strapped upright to a sled on long rails, with a row of rockets lighting behind him.
card.inside: His glass head and chest as the sled stops: held by the harness, his brain stays clear; without it, the same stop in the first short.
needs: a person
a rocket sled
rails
a harness
a water brake
card.source: John Stapp's 1954 Sonic Wind run, US Air Force; the 2003 Ig Nobel in engineering

card.topic: Why castles stopped being tall, and turned into stars
card.hook: A castle said to have once held out for seven years falls in eight hours.
card.people_think: Higher, thicker walls are always stronger.
card.truth: A tall stone wall is the perfect target for a cannon: hit its base and its own weight brings it down. So forts went low, backed with earth, and then shaped like stars so nothing could hide.
steps: Walls were tall so ladders couldn't reach the top.
A cannonball hits the base, and the tall wall falls under its own weight and fills the ditch with a ramp.
So builders sank walls low and backed them with packed earth, which swallows a cannonball instead of shattering.
But a round tower has a blind spot at its foot, where attackers can stand safely.
So towers became sharp angles, each one firing along the face of the next, and the whole fort from above is a star.
card.turn: They worked so well that armies stopped rushing them, and spent weeks digging zigzag trenches towards them instead.

card.inside: A cut through the wall, stone against packed earth taking the same cannonball; from above, lines of fire as glowing lines reaching every spot.

card.topic: The reason planes fly that your teacher got wrong
card.hook: If wings worked the way most schools teach, no plane could ever fly upside down.
card.people_think: Air over the curved top has further to go, so it speeds up to meet the air below, and that's what makes the lift.
card.truth: The air doesn't meet up at all. A wing works by turning air downwards: bending the flow lowers the pressure on top and raises it below, and that pushes the wing up.
steps: The school version says air over the top must catch up with the air below.
Measure it, and the air over the top gets there first and never meets it.
If the longer path over the top did the work, flipping a wing would pull the plane into the ground.
A wing tilted into the air pushes air down whichever way up it is.
Pushing air down pushes the wing up, the same thing your hand feels out of a car window.
card.turn: That pushed-down air rolls into invisible tornadoes behind a big jet, strong enough to flip a small plane following it.
card.first_picture: A stunt plane flying level, upside down, the pilot hanging in the straps.
card.inside: Air as moving balls round a cut through the wing, bending down behind it.
needs: a plane
a wing cut in half
a person
card.source: NASA Glenn Research Center, incorrect lift theories

card.topic: The dead fish that swam upstream

card.truth: Behind a post, water spins off in whirlpools, left then right. A floppy body bending in them gets pushed forward, with no brain or muscle at all.
steps: Water passing a post sheds whirlpools, one to the left, then one to the right.
Each whirlpool bends the soft body as it goes past.
The bent body meets the next whirlpool at an angle, like a wing, and that angle gives a push forward.
So it creeps towards the post against the current, and its line goes slack.
card.turn: Live trout do this too: behind a post, they stop using most of their swimming muscles, and for moments all of them.

card.topic: Why toast lands butter down, and why the universe decided it
card.hook: Knock your toast off the table and it usually lands butter down, and the strength of atoms decided that.
card.people_think: The butter makes that side heavier, or you only remember the bad times.
card.truth: It's the spin. Toast tips over the table's edge and starts turning, and from table height it only has time for about half a turn.
steps: Toast sliding off an edge tips, and gravity sets it turning as it goes.
It turns slowly: about half a turn by the time it reaches the floor.
So butter up ends up butter down, and the butter's too light to matter.
A table about three metres tall would give it time to come round butter-up.
Tables suit our height, and our height is limited, since a person much taller would break their skull falling over, and how hard a skull is comes down to the forces between atoms.
card.turn: So you can't fix it: the people tall enough for a toast-safe table couldn't survive tripping over.

card.topic: The frog that floated in mid-air
card.hook: A live frog floats in mid-air inside a magnet, touching nothing, and then hops away unharmed.
card.people_think: Magnets only pull on iron, and a frog has nothing magnetic in it.
card.truth: Everything is slightly magnetic. Water is very weakly pushed away by a magnet, and a magnet thousands of times stronger than a fridge magnet makes that push beat gravity.
steps: A magnetic field makes the electrons in every atom set up a tiny field of their own, pointing against it.
That pushes the atom away from the magnet, so weakly that you never notice.
A frog is mostly water, and water gets that push.
At 16 tesla, the push on every bit of water matches gravity, and since every bit is held up at once, nothing inside is squashed.
card.turn: The man who did it won a joke Ig Nobel for it, and a real Nobel ten years later, the only individual to win both. And you're mostly water too.

card.topic: Why a bullet can't throw someone backwards
card.hook: If a bullet could throw a man across the room, it would throw the shooter across the room too.
card.people_think: It happens in every film: a bullet's so powerful that it knocks you off your feet.
card.truth: A bullet carries no more push than the kick the gun gave the shooter's shoulder, and the shooter stays standing.
steps: A gun pushes a bullet forwards and the bullet pushes the gun back, exactly as hard.
The shooter takes all of that in the shoulder and stays on their feet.
The bullet can't hand over more push than that.
So as a shove, a hit is no bigger than the gun's kick, and people go down for other reasons.

card.topic: Why a giraffe doesn't faint when it lifts its head
card.hook: A giraffe lifts its head from the water to five metres up, and it doesn't faint.
card.people_think: It has a long neck and a big heart, so the heart just pumps harder.
card.truth: The pressure is only half of it. Its body is built like a pressure suit, with tight skin on its legs and valves in its neck.
steps: To get blood two metres up its neck, its heart runs at about twice our pressure.
That same pressure at its feet would swell its legs, so the skin there is tight like a compression sock.
Bending down would let blood run back up its neck veins, so one-way valves stop it.
Lifting it again would drain its head, so the blood vessels in its brain widen and pressure sensors hold its blood pressure up.
card.turn: Pilots wear the same idea in a g-suit, a squeeze on the legs.

card.inside: A glass giraffe with its blood as a red flow, valves closing in its neck.

a pool of water
card.source: Hargens et al., Gravitational haemodynamics and oedema prevention in the giraffe, Nature, 1987

card.topic: The frog whose heart stops all winter

card.truth: The ice forms between its cells, not inside them. The frog floods its cells with sugar, which keeps them from freezing, so they survive with up to about two thirds of its water turned to ice.
steps: Ice touching its skin sets its liver dumping sugar into its blood within minutes.
The sugar fills its cells, and syrup doesn't freeze easily.
Ice grows in the spaces between the cells and draws water out of them.
Its heart and breathing stop, and its cells get by on stored fuel until the thaw.
card.turn: When it thaws, its heart starts by itself, and transplant researchers have borrowed the trick to keep rat livers partly frozen five times longer.

card.goal: Make a balloon push a plane, and never run out.
steps: It's flat in two seconds and the plane drops, so you stop carrying air and grab it from in front with a spinning fan in a tube: the compressor.
The fan alone gives a feeble push, so you spray fuel into the squeezed air and light it, and it swells and blasts out of the back: the burner.
The engine spinning the fan weighs as much as an ordinary engine giving the same push, so you put a windmill in the blast on the fan's own shaft, and the fire spins its own fan: the turbine.

It's deafening and gulps fuel, so a second turbine at the back, on a shaft running inside the first, turns a giant fan at the front that blows most of the air round the outside, for more push from the same fuel: the turbofan.
card.seen_it: Under the wings of most airliners, and roaring at any airport.
card.inside: The engine cut in half lengthways: air as blue balls squeezed through rows of blades, the flame in the middle, the turbines spun by the blast, the inner shaft glowing to show the back turbine turning the fan.

an airliner
a jet engine cut in half: fan, compressor blades, burner, and two turbines on two shafts, one inside the other
a piston engine spinning a fan in a tube
air as moving balls
a flame and a hot blast
a fuel gauge dropping
card.ending: An airliner lifting off, one engine cut open to show the giant fan, the blades squeezing the air, the flame and both turbines turning at once: "Congratulations, you just built a jet engine."

card.hook: Put a brick on a wall. Now make the wall three hundred metres tall.
card.first_picture: A hand setting one brick on top of a low brick wall.
card.everyday: Lifting a brick, a box or a block up onto something taller.
card.goal: Get the bricks to the top as the tower grows.
steps: You can't reach, so you stand a tall pole beside the wall with a rope over a wheel at the top: the mast and hoist.

A heavy load out on the arm tips the whole tower over, so a short arm sticks out of the back stacked with concrete blocks: the counterweight.

Past about 80 metres it can't stand on its own, so as it climbs it's tied to the building with steel collars: the tie-ins.

card.topic: A playground slide made a hundred times taller, fixed step by step into a roller coaster
card.hook: Whoosh down a playground slide. Now make it a hundred times taller.
card.first_picture: A playground slide, a grown-up whooshing down it.
card.goal: Ride the giant slide safely, and go again.
steps: Straight down from that height you'd hit the ground as fast as a racing car, so at the bottom the rails swoop back up and your speed carries you up the next hill instead of into the ground, in a car with wheels on rails: the track.
Over the top of a hill the car flies up off the rails, so a second set of wheels runs underneath the rail and holds it on: the upstop wheels.

At the end you're at the bottom, and someone has to haul you back up (on a Pennsylvania coal railway that became one of the first rides, mules did it), so a motor drags the car up the first hill on a chain: the lift hill.
If the chain snaps, the car rolls backwards down the hill, so a hook under the car rides up over teeth beside the chain and catches if it rolls back: the anti-rollback, clack, clack, clack.
card.seen_it: At every theme park and fair, clacking up its first hill.
card.cycle: chain up, clack, drop, swoop, again
card.inside: The car from the side with the rail cut through: running wheels on top, upstop wheels underneath; the hook dropping into the teeth in close-up on the lift hill.

a roller coaster car with running wheels and upstop wheels
track with a lift hill, hills and dips
a chain and motor
anti-rollback teeth and a hook
a crash-test dummy in the car

card.topic: A thumb over a hose, fixed step by step into the sprinkler whose own jet knocks it round
card.hook: Put your thumb over a hose. Now water a whole football pitch.
card.first_picture: A thumb over the end of a garden hose, the water fanning out across a lawn.
card.everyday: Putting a thumb over a garden hose so the water sprays further.
card.goal: Water the whole pitch without standing there.
steps: You'd stand there all day, so you fix a nozzle on a stand, and it drowns one spot while the rest goes brown: the sprinkler head.
It has to turn slowly, a step at a time, so the long jet sweeps a whole circle, but there's no motor, so the jet itself hits a spoon on a swinging arm and knocks it away: the drive arm.
The arm would just stay out, so a spring snaps it back, and it whacks the nozzle round one small step and swings back into the jet: the arm spring.
The jet flies over the grass close by, which stays dry, so a pin pokes into the jet and breaks some of it into spray: the diffuser pin.

card.cycle: jet hits, arm flies, spring snaps back
card.inside: Slow motion close up: the jet striking the spoon, the arm swinging out, the spring glowing as it pulls the arm back to strike the nozzle, the nozzle stepping round a notch.

a football pitch of grass, brown where it's dry
impact sprinklers: one in close-up (nozzle, drive arm with spoon, spring, diffuser pin), and six or more round the pitch
a water jet and spray
a person holding a hose, half asleep

card.topic: The owner's idea: why a touchscreen ignores your gloved finger
card.hook: Put gloves on in winter and your phone's screen ignores you, however hard you press.
card.first_picture: A thick woollen glove pressing hard on a phone screen, and the screen doing nothing.
card.people_think: The screen feels you pressing, so a glove is just too thick or too soft to press it properly.
card.truth: The screen doesn't find your finger by pressing at all. Under the glass is a grid of see-through wires holding a little electric charge, and a bare fingertip draws some of that charge away into your body. A woollen or leather glove holds your fingertip a few millimetres further from the wires, through fibre and air that carry no charge, so it draws away far too little for the phone to count.
steps: Under the glass are two layers of see-through wires, made of indium tin oxide: rows on one layer, columns on the other, crossing in a grid.
The phone charges one row at a time, and at every crossing some of that charge reaches across to the column.
A bare fingertip near a crossing draws some of the charge away into your body, so less reaches that column.
The phone charges every row in turn, over and over, finds the crossing that came up short, and that's where you touched.
A glove holds your fingertip a few millimetres further off, through wool or leather that carry no charge, so it draws away too little charge for the phone to notice, however hard you press.
card.turn: Anything big, wet and salty draws charge like a finger. In South Korea's cold winter of 2010, phone users kept their gloves on and tapped with snack sausages, and the sausages' maker told a newspaper the sausage's convenience-store sales that December and January were up 39% on the same months a year before.
card.ending: A glove with a patch of conductive thread sewn into its fingertip taps the screen, and the screen answers. Said: give the charge a path through the glove, and the screen finds your finger again.
card.inside: A cut through the glass: rows and columns of thin glowing wire, charge as small balls crossing at each junction, a bright line sweeping row by row; a bare fingertip pulls balls away at one crossing and that spot lights up; a woollen glove as a thick gap that only a few balls reach across, too few to light the spot; the conductive thread as a bridge they can.
needs: a person's hand
a phone
a woollen glove
a touchscreen glove with conductive thread in the fingertip
a snack sausage
a cutaway of the glass with its wire grid
charge as moving balls
card.source: How the grid works: Apple's patent US 7,663,607, Multipoint touchscreen (Hotelling, Strickon and Huppi; filed 2004, granted 2010): ITO lines, rows driven one at a time, 'the object steals charge'. Gloves: background of US 9,851,794, Bulk resistive glove (2017); gloved fingers detected through thin gloves with a more sensitive scan: https://patents.google.com/patent/US9778742B2/en. Sausages: Etoday (Korea), 9 Feb 2010, quoting CJ CheilJedang's brand manager on Maxbong sales, Dec 2009 to Jan 2010.

card.topic: A brick on a wall, fixed step by step into the tower crane that climbs its own tower
card.hook: Put a brick on a wall. Now make the wall three hundred metres tall.
card.first_picture: A hand setting one brick on top of a low brick wall.
card.everyday: Lifting a brick, a box or a block up onto something taller.
card.goal: Get the bricks to the top as the tower grows.
steps: You can't reach, so you stand a tall pole beside the wall with a rope over a wheel at the top: the mast and hoist.
It only lifts straight up beside the pole, so you lay a long arm across the top with a trolley that runs out along it: the jib.
A heavy load out on the arm tips the whole tower over, so a short arm sticks out of the back stacked with concrete blocks: the counterweight.
It can only reach one side, so the arms sit on a giant turntable and swing all the way round: the slewing ring.
The building grows past the crane, so a frame round the tower jacks the top up, and the crane hoists the next piece of its own tower into the gap and bolts it in: the climbing frame.
Past about 80 metres it can't stand on its own, so as it climbs it's tied to the building with steel collars: the tie-ins.

card.cycle: jack up, hoist in, bolt, repeat

card.topic: A wheelbarrow sinking in mud, fixed step by step into the caterpillar track
card.hook: A wheelbarrow sinks into mud. Now make it as heavy as a lorry.
card.first_picture: A wheelbarrow full of bricks, its wheel sunk to the axle in mud.
card.everyday: Pushing a loaded wheelbarrow, pram or bike onto soft ground and the wheel sinking in.
card.goal: Get a machine as heavy as a lorry across a bog.
steps: All the weight presses on one small patch of mud, so you make the wheels wider: Benjamin Holt's steam tractor, before 1904, got wheels sticking 18 feet out on each side, and it couldn't fit through a gate, cross a bridge or turn round, and it still sank.
So you lay planks on the mud to spread the weight, as armies did in the Boer War, but someone has to keep carrying the last plank round to the front.
So you fix the planks round the wheel's rim, and the wheel lays its own as it rolls: the endless railway wheel, 1846.
So you bolt the planks to a chain loop round the wheels, and a toothed wheel turns it, laying planks down in front and picking them up behind: the track.

card.cycle: lay down, roll over, pick up, carry round
card.inside: A cut through the mud: a red glow of pressure under the one sinking wheel, spread to a faint glow under the whole track; the track loop see-through so the toothed wheel and rollers show.

card.hook: Whoosh down a playground slide. Now make it a hundred times taller.
card.first_picture: A playground slide, a grown-up whooshing down it.
card.goal: Ride the giant slide safely, and go again.
steps: Straight down from that height you'd hit the ground as fast as a racing car, so at the bottom the rails swoop back up and your speed carries you up the next hill instead of into the ground, in a car with wheels on rails: the track.
Over the top of a hill the car flies up off the rails, so a second set of wheels runs underneath the rail and holds it on: the upstop wheels.

If the chain snaps, the car rolls backwards down the hill, so a hook under the car rides up over teeth beside the chain and catches if it rolls back: the anti-rollback, clack, clack, clack.

card.cycle: chain up, clack, drop, swoop, again

card.hook: Put your thumb over a hose. Now water a whole football pitch.
card.first_picture: A thumb over the end of a garden hose, the water fanning out across a lawn.
card.everyday: Putting a thumb over a garden hose so the water sprays further.
card.goal: Water the whole pitch without standing there.
steps: You'd stand there all day, so you fix a nozzle on a stand, and it drowns one spot while the rest goes brown: the sprinkler head.
It has to turn slowly, a step at a time, so the long jet sweeps a whole circle, but there's no motor, so the jet itself hits a spoon on a swinging arm and knocks it away: the drive arm.
The arm would just stay out, so a spring snaps it back, and it whacks the nozzle round one small step and swings back into the jet: the arm spring.
The jet flies over the grass close by, which stays dry, so a pin pokes into the jet and breaks some of it into spray: the diffuser pin.

a football pitch of grass, brown where it's dry

card.topic: The owner's idea: why a touchscreen ignores your gloved finger
card.hook: Put gloves on in winter and your phone's screen ignores you, however hard you press.
card.first_picture: A thick woollen glove pressing hard on a phone screen, and the screen doing nothing.
card.people_think: The screen feels you pressing, so a glove is just too thick or too soft to press it properly.
card.truth: The screen doesn't find your finger by pressing at all. Under the glass is a grid of see-through wires holding a little electric charge, and a bare fingertip draws some of that charge away into your body. A woollen or leather glove holds your fingertip a few millimetres further from the wires, through fibre and air that carry no charge, so it draws away far too little for the phone to count.
steps: Under the glass are two layers of see-through wires, made of indium tin oxide: rows on one layer, columns on the other, crossing in a grid.
The phone charges one row at a time, and at every crossing some of that charge reaches across to the column.
A bare fingertip near a crossing draws some of the charge away into your body, so less reaches that column.
The phone charges every row in turn, over and over, finds the crossing that came up short, and that's where you touched.
A glove holds your fingertip a few millimetres further off, through wool or leather that carry no charge, so it draws away too little charge for the phone to notice, however hard you press.
card.turn: Anything big, wet and salty draws charge like a finger. In South Korea's cold winter of 2010, phone users kept their gloves on and tapped with snack sausages, and the sausages' maker told a newspaper the sausage's convenience-store sales that December and January were up 39% on the same months a year before.
card.ending: A glove with a patch of conductive thread sewn into its fingertip taps the screen, and the screen answers. Said: give the charge a path through the glove, and the screen finds your finger again.
card.inside: A cut through the glass: rows and columns of thin glowing wire, charge as small balls crossing at each junction, a bright line sweeping row by row; a bare fingertip pulls balls away at one crossing and that spot lights up; a woollen glove as a thick gap that only a few balls reach across, too few to light the spot; the conductive thread as a bridge they can.

entries.idea: Why fruit growers spray their blossom with water on a freezing night
their_words: yea seems interesting

card.topic: Why fruit growers spray their blossom with water on a freezing night
card.hook: It's freezing tonight, and this farmer is spraying his apple blossom with water.
card.first_picture: An apple tree in blossom at night, every branch and flower cased in clear ice with icicles hanging, and a sprinkler still spraying water over it.
card.people_think: Ice is what kills a plant, so wetting it on a freezing night is the worst thing you could do. Or, at a guess, the ice must wrap the flower like a blanket.
card.truth: Water gives out heat as it turns to ice. As long as fresh water keeps landing and freezing on the flower, that heat holds the flower at about 0 C, while the air around it drops to the temperatures that kill open apple blossom (about -2 C starts killing it, about -4 C kills most of it).
steps: On a clear, still spring night the air in the orchard falls below freezing, and open apple blossom starts to die at about -2 C.
The grower turns on sprinklers over the trees, and water lands on every flower.
As each bit of water freezes it gives out heat: 334 kilojoules for every kilogram, straight into the flower it's freezing on.
While there's still wet water on top of the ice, the flower inside stays at about 0 C, while the air around it goes on getting colder.
So the sprinklers must keep running all night: clear ice with water dripping off it means enough water is arriving, and milky white ice means too little.
card.turn: Do it badly and it's worse than doing nothing. Kilo for kilo, water that evaporates takes away about seven and a half times the heat that freezing gives out, so if the sprinklers stop early or spray too little, the wet flower falls well below the air's temperature and dies sooner than a dry one. And the ice gets heavy enough to snap branches.
card.ending: Morning sun on the orchard: the ice melts and drips off, and the blossom under it is white and whole, beside an unsprayed tree whose blossom has gone brown. Said: the ice was never a blanket. The freezing was the heater.
card.inside: A cut through one flower in its shell of ice: a wet film on the outside, each drop that freezes giving off a small warm glow into the flower; a thermometer badge inside the ice holding at 0 while a second badge in the air falls to -4; then the sprinkler stops, the wet film steams away as small balls leaving the surface, and the inside badge drops below the air's.

an orchard sprinkler
water drops and a shell of clear ice with icicles
a cutaway of one flower inside the ice

two thermometer badges

card.topic: Why Utah drops thousands of live fish out of a plane
card.hook: A plane skims a mountain lake and dumps thousands of live fish out.
card.first_picture: A small plane low over a mountain lake, a long white cloud of water and tiny fish pouring out from under its belly.
card.people_think: It's a stunt, or the fish must die when they hit: a fall like that onto water would kill anything.
card.truth: It's how Utah's wildlife agency stocks more than 300 mountain lakes a year that no road reaches. Only fish 1 to 3 inches long are dropped, because for something that small the air slows the fall, so they land gently. The agency's biologists have netted lakes minutes after a drop and report high survival, and say bigger fish would not survive as well.
steps: The lakes sit high in the mountains with no road to them, so a hatchery truck can't get there.
So the young fish, 1 to 3 inches long, go into a tank in the plane's belly: more than 10,000 of them a flight, in seven chambers with hundreds of pounds of water.
The pilot comes in 50 to 150 feet above the lake and opens one chamber, and fish and water pour out together.
A fish that small weighs almost nothing for the amount of air it has to push through, so the air slows its drop and it flutters down instead of plunging.
It lands, and swims off. A bigger fish falls harder, which is why only the small ones go by air.
card.turn: It isn't the desperate option. The agency says dropping them from a plane would still be the cheaper way even if every one of those lakes had a road, and it has done it since at least 1956. Before the planes, by its own account in press reports, the fish went up in metal milk cans tied to pack horses.
card.ending: The fingerlings hit the water in a patter of small splashes and dart away, while the plane banks toward the next lake with six chambers still shut. Said: a fish this small falls slowly enough that nearly all of them survive. That's the whole trick, and it's why only the small ones fly.
card.inside: The plane's belly cut open to show the tank's seven chambers and one door opening; then the fall slowed right down: one fingerling beside a big trout dropped from the same height, air as moving balls piling up under each, a speed badge on each with no numbers, the small one's reading slower and the big one's faster.

entries.idea: Why road crews fire army howitzers at snowy mountains
their_words: must be about things that still exist today

card.topic: Why road crews fire army howitzers at snowy mountains
card.hook: A road crew aims an army howitzer at a mountain, and fires.
card.first_picture: A 105 mm howitzer on a platform beside an empty snowy highway, its barrel pointed up at a slope loaded with snow.
card.people_think: They're blasting the snow off the mountain, or stopping an avalanche from happening.
card.truth: They're causing the avalanche, on purpose, early. A slab of snow slides when a crack about a foot long opens in a weak layer underneath it and runs across the slope, and an explosion can make that crack. So the crew empties the road, fires a shell into the top of the slope, and brings the snow down while it's still a small slide and nobody is under it.
steps: Snow lies on the mountain in layers, and sometimes a strong slab sits on top of a weak, crumbly layer.
Every storm adds weight, until a crack opens in the weak layer. Once it's about a foot long it runs across the slope, the slab comes loose, and it slides down onto the road.
Nobody can say which minute that will happen, and the longer it waits the more snow comes down.
So the crew closes the highway, clears every car out, and fires a 105 mm shell into the top of the slope.
The blast makes that crack itself, and the slab slides now, small, onto an empty road. A plough clears it, and the road reopens, usually within 30 minutes to two hours.
card.turn: The guns are surplus military artillery: by a ski-industry report, they belong to the US Army and are lent out through the Forest Service, and the shells are running out because the Army has stopped using them. So the howitzers are being swapped for towers on the mountain that drop a charge by remote control. Washington's Snoqualmie Pass fired its last rounds before the 2025 winter.
card.ending: The highway open again, cars driving past a ploughed heap of snow at the foot of a bare slide path, the howitzer under its cover. Said: they never stopped the avalanche. They chose the minute it fell.
card.inside: A cut through the snow on the slope: a thick slab over a thin crumbly layer, the bedrock under both; a weight badge on the slab growing with each storm; the shell landing and a ring of force pushing down, a bright crack opening in the weak layer and racing sideways across the slope; then the slab sliding as one sheet.

their_words: i also dont get the live power line from helicopter, is it to charge the hleicopter or what

card.topic: Why a lineman can grab a live high-voltage line from a helicopter
card.hook: A man leans out of a helicopter and grabs a live power line.
card.first_picture: A helicopter hovering level with a thick power cable, a lineman in a silvery suit on a platform at its side, holding a metal wand out to the cable as a spark jumps to it.
card.people_think: The line must be switched off, or his suit and gloves are thick rubber that keeps the electricity out.
card.truth: The line is live and his suit is made to carry electricity, not block it. Electricity only flows through you when you touch two things at different voltages. The helicopter touches nothing but air, so once it's joined to the line, the man, the helicopter and the line are all at the same voltage, and nothing flows through him. He is, in the US safety agency's words, 'literally charged to the same voltage as the line'.
steps: Electricity flows through a body only when it bridges two things at different voltages, like the line and the ground.
The helicopter hovers beside the line touching nothing but air, so it has no path to the ground.
The lineman reaches out a metal wand: a spark jumps as the helicopter and everyone on it are charged up to the line's voltage.
He clamps a wire from the platform to the line, so they stay joined. Now there's no difference between him and the line, and nothing flows through him.
His suit is woven to conduct, so the charge runs round the outside of him instead of through him, and he works on the live cable with his hands.
card.turn: It's the bird on the wire, and it holds only while he touches nothing else: reach from the line toward the steel tower, which is joined to the ground, and the full voltage is across him. They do it this way because the line can't be spared: Idaho Power says switching lines off for repairs is harder and harder to get permission for, and one job its helicopter crews did live in 15 days would have taken a ground crew about three and a half months.
card.ending: The clamp comes off, a last spark jumps from the wand, and the helicopter peels away from a line that was never switched off, towns lit below. Said: safe as a bird on a wire, as long as he touched nothing else. And the lights never went out.

entries.idea: Why live chicks can be posted in a box with no food or water
their_words: goooooood

card.topic: Why live chicks can be posted in a box with no food or water
card.hook: Live chicks come by post in a box with no food or water.
card.first_picture: A cardboard box with round air holes on a post office counter, small yellow chick heads and beaks poking out of the holes, a parcel label on its side.
card.people_think: That it must be cruel or a mistake: a baby animal a day old, shut in a box for up to three days with nothing to eat or drink, should arrive dead or starving.
card.truth: A chick hatches with its food already inside it. Just before hatching it takes what is left of the egg's yolk into its own belly, and that yolk feeds and waters it for the first days. So hatcheries post chicks on the day they hatch, and the US Postal Service's rules give the box 72 hours from hatching to arrive.
steps: A hatchery packs chicks into a ventilated box on the day they hatch: by the postal rules they must be no more than 24 hours old.
The box holds no food and no water, and the rules give it until 72 hours after hatching to be delivered, with the hour of hatching written on its side.
Just before a chick breaks out of its egg, it draws the last of the egg's yolk into its own belly.
That yolk is rich in energy and water, so the chick lives on it for its first days and doesn't need to eat or drink yet.
As the hours pass the yolk is used up, so the box has to arrive before it runs out, and the first thing the chicks are given is water and feed.
card.turn: The yolk was never meant for the post. Eggs under a hen don't all hatch at once, and she can't leave the nest until the last one is out, so the first chicks out have to wait under her with nothing to eat. That wait is up to about two days. The post office stretches it to three. And it's a hard limit: a Purdue University article warns that when a box takes longer than 72 hours, the chicks are in danger.
card.ending: The box is opened at a farm and the chicks tumble out and go straight to a dish of water, one seen in x-ray with its yolk much smaller. Said: every chick hatches with enough yolk inside it to last about three days. The post office has three days to get it there.
card.inside: An x-ray of one chick in the box: the yellow yolk inside its belly, big at the start, with a clock badge counting from 0 to 72 hours as the yolk shrinks. Then a cut through an egg just before hatching, the chick drawing the yolk in. Then a nest under a hen: two chicks already out and waiting beside eggs that haven't hatched yet.

day-old chicks
a post office counter

a dish of water and feed
card.source: US Postal Service, Publication 52, section 526.3, Live Day-Old Poultry: chickens, ducks, geese, turkeys and others mailable; 'Poultry must be no more than 24 hours old'; in the hatchery's original unopened box with proper ventilation; 'may be delivered to the addressee within 72 hours of the time of hatching'; the section says nothing of food or water. Still done today: USPS Postal Bulletin 22706, 9 Jul 2026, revised this very rule (boxes to carry the hatching date and hour and the words 'Delivery is expected within 72 hours of hatching'): https://about.usps.com/postal-bulletin/2026/pb22706/html/updt_001.htm ; and The Alpena News, 24 Mar 2025, on a Michigan post office handling about 150 boxes of chicks a year. No food or water in the box, and the yolk: Purdue University, 4 Aug 2020, quoting poultry scientists at Purdue, Virginia Tech and Maryland ('a specially ventilated box ... without any source of food or water'; 'Chicks can survive a few days after hatching without food and water through their yolk reserves'; delays past 72 hours endanger them): https://ag.purdue.edu/news/2020/08/you-can-order-live-poultry-through-the-mail-but-should-you.html That the yolk is taken into the belly just before hatching, lasts up to three days, and lets early chicks wait while the hen finishes hatching the rest: the hatchery My Pet Chicken's own explanation (a seller, not a study): https://www.mypetchicken.com/blogs/faqs/how-come-you-can-only-ship-chicks-when-theyre-one-day-old That the yolk is 'rich in energy and moisture' and sustains a chick up to 72 hours is from a University of California extension leaflet seen only in a search summary, not opened. Studies find chicks kept 48 hours without feed and water lose weight, so 72 hours is a limit, not a comfortable allowance. Added by the fact-check, Nov 11, 2026: junglefowl hens stay on the nest until the last chick is out, early chicks living on yolk up to two days (The Poultry Site, 2016: https://www.thepoultrysite.com/news/2016/07/using-nature-as-a-reference-to-optimise-welfare-and-performance); unfed chicks held 72 hours used just over 80% of their yolk (Aviagen brief, seen in summary). The University of California leaflet was never opened and isn't relied on.

entries.idea: Why rescuers tie big floats to a whale that's already tangled in rope
their_words: i thik just add all of them to backlog

card.topic: Why rescuers tie big floats to a whale that's already tangled in rope
card.hook: This whale is tangled in rope, so rescuers tie big floats to it.
card.first_picture: A whale's back and tail at the surface wrapped in rope, a small inflatable boat close behind it, and a line of big orange buoys dragging in the water from the rope.
card.people_think: That it's backwards: the whale is already dragging rope it can't shake off, and they're adding more weight and more drag. Surely you'd dive in and cut it free.
card.truth: A tangled whale is free-swimming and far too strong to hold, and it can dive and swim away from a boat. So the team hooks the rope it's trailing and clips large floats to it. The floats add lift and drag, so the whale finds it hard to dive and tires, and stays near the surface moving slowly. Only then can a small boat get close enough to cut the rope with a hooked knife on a long pole.
steps: A whale swims with fishing rope wrapped round its tail, and it can dive and swim away from any boat that comes close.
From a small inflatable boat the team throws a grapple, a hook on a line, that catches the rope trailing behind the whale.
They clip large floats onto that line, and the floats pull up and drag through the water behind the whale.
Now the whale finds it hard to dive and has to pull the floats along, so it tires, slows down and stays at the surface.
The boat comes up close behind it, and a hook-shaped knife on a thirty-foot pole reaches out and cuts the rope from the tail.
The rope and the floats fall away together, and the whale swims off.
card.turn: The trick comes from whaling. Whalers called it kegging: they harpooned a whale and tied wooden kegs to the line, to wear it out and hold it at the surface. The rescuers kept the floats and swapped the weapon for a knife that cuts rope. It doesn't always work: in January 2026 a young right whale off the US coast, slowed with buoys and a sea anchor, still swam away with rope round its tail.
card.ending: The last wrap of rope is cut, the orange floats bob loose on the surface, and the whale lifts its tail and dives. Said: the floats were never there to save it. They were there to slow it down long enough for one cut.
card.inside: A view from the side, half above and half under the water: the whale diving freely with the rope, then the floats added and a lift arrow at each float and a drag arrow behind it, the whale's dive getting shallower each time until it stays at the top; a speed badge with no numbers falling. Then the old picture beside it: a wooden whaleboat and kegs on a line, the same shape.

a small inflatable boat with two people in helmets and life jackets

lift and drag arrows
a wooden whaleboat with kegs on a line

The steps (grappling hooks attaching working ropes, buoys added 'to slow the whale and keep it at the surface', a hooked knife on a long pole) are from the Center's report of an 11-hour rescue on 2 Aug 2015. Still done today: the Center's report of 20 Jan 2026 (large buoys and a sea anchor added to a yearling right whale's entanglement to slow it; part of the gear broke away and the whale left with rope round its tail): https://coastalstudies.org/?p=19047 ; its report of 15 Jun 2026 (a humpback freed with 'a hook-shaped knife at the end of a thirty-foot pole'); and the San Juan Journal, 6 Sep 2025, on Cascadia Research Collective and The Whale Museum kegging a young humpback on 21 Aug 2025 ('adding large buoys to slow the whale and keep it at the surface'). That whalers fastened kegs to whales to tire them and keep them up is NOAA's account as given in a search summary, not opened; the Center's own page says only 'an old whaling practice'. That the boat comes up close behind once the whale is slow is how the reports read; the exact way the boat closes the distance is not spelled out in what was read. The first picture shows no wound on the whale.

card.topic: Why zookeepers keep taking a newborn cub away from a panda with twins
card.hook: A zookeeper is taking a newborn cub away from its mother panda.
card.first_picture: A giant panda sitting with a tiny pink cub held against her chest, and a keeper's gloved hand lifting a second tiny pink cub away from beside her.
card.people_think: That taking a newborn from its mother is the worst thing you could do to it, and that a mother with twins would simply raise both.
card.truth: A panda has twins about half the time, but she can hold and nurse only one newborn at a time, and the other is left. So keepers put one twin in a warm incubator and leave her the other, and every few hours they swap them. She only ever has one cub to hold, and both get her milk.
steps: A giant panda gives birth to twins about half the time, and each newborn is tiny: about 90 to 140 grams, pink and helpless.
A newborn has to be held against her and put in place to feed. She can do that for one cub, and the second is left lying apart.
So keepers lift one cub away and put it in an incubator, where it's kept warm and fed from a bottle.
A few hours later they swap: the cub from the incubator goes to the mother, and the one she was holding goes to the incubator.
The swap is repeated day and night, so she only ever has one cub to hold, and both cubs get their turn at her milk and both grow.
card.turn: It only works if she lets go. At the Smithsonian's National Zoo in 2015 the mother, Mei Xiang, sometimes would not put down the cub she was holding, and the keepers could only wait with the other one in the incubator. The zoo's own words: much of their method 'will be dictated by Mei Xiang'.
card.ending: Two round black-and-white cubs at two months old, side by side, one heavier than the other by a little, their mother behind them holding one. Said: she never raised two cubs at once. She raised one at a time, twice, and never knew.
card.inside: The den seen from above with two places lit: the mother's arms and the incubator. A cub in each, a small milk badge filling beside whichever cub is with the mother and a warm glow round the one in the incubator; a clock badge turns, the cubs change places, and the other cub's milk badge fills. Two weight badges climb together.

That Mei Xiang at times would not put a cub down, delaying swaps, is from news reports of Aug 2015 (NBC Washington, CBS) read as search summaries. News reports also say a mother lacks the milk for two; no zoo source read confirms it, so it's left out. The smaller of the 2015 National Zoo twins died days later; the method raises the odds, it doesn't guarantee both.

entries.idea: Why a baby born very early is put straight into a plastic bag, still wet
their_words: i thik just add all of them to backlog

card.topic: Why a baby born very early is put straight into a plastic bag, still wet
card.hook: A tiny newborn has just been slid into a clear plastic bag.
card.first_picture: A very small newborn baby under a warming lamp, its body inside a clear plastic bag up to the neck, its head outside the bag in a small knitted hat, a nurse's gloved hands closing the bag.
card.people_think: That a plastic bag is the last thing you'd put a baby in, and that a wet newborn should be rubbed dry and wrapped in a warm blanket.
card.truth: A baby born more than eight weeks early arrives wet, and the water drying off its skin carries its heat away faster than its small body can make more. Drying it with a towel takes time and leaves the skin bare. So the team dries only the head, puts on a hat, and slides the wet body into a polythene bag up to the neck. The water can't leave the bag, so the heat stays in the baby.
steps: A baby born before 32 weeks arrives very small and wet, into a room far cooler than the womb.
As the water on its skin dries off into the air, it takes heat from the baby with it, and the baby's temperature starts to fall.
So the team doesn't dry the body. They dry only the head and put a hat on it, and slide the wet body into a clear polythene bag up to the neck.
Inside the bag the water has nowhere to go, so it stops carrying heat away, and a warming lamp above keeps heating the baby through the bag.
The baby's temperature holds: in the trial that started it, bagged babies reached the ward at 36.5 C on average, and towel-dried babies at 35.6 C.
card.turn: It works well enough to cause the opposite problem. Across the trials, about 12 in every 1,000 babies cared for the usual way got too hot, and about 46 in every 1,000 of the bagged ones did. So a thermometer stays on the baby the whole time, and the aim is a narrow band: 36.5 to 37.5 C.
card.ending: The baby lies in an incubator, still in its bag and hat, with a thermometer badge reading 37.0 beside it, and beside that the same scene without the bag, the badge falling. Said: the cold room wasn't the danger. Drying off was. So they don't let the baby dry.
card.inside: Close on the baby's wet skin: water leaving it as small balls rising into the air, each one carrying off a small warm glow, a thermometer badge falling. Then the bag closes round the body: the balls rise, meet the plastic and stay inside, the glow stays on the baby, and warmth from the lamp above comes down through the bag. The badge holds.

entries.idea: Why fire crews set fire to the ground under giant sequoias
their_words: i thik just add all of them to backlog

card.topic: Why fire crews set fire to the ground under giant sequoias
card.hook: These firefighters are setting fire to the ground under the world's biggest trees.
card.first_picture: The huge red trunk of a giant sequoia, a firefighter small at its foot, and a line of low flame spreading across the forest floor toward the trunk from where the firefighter stands.
card.people_think: That fire is the one thing these trees need protecting from, so the job is to put every fire out. Lighting one on purpose looks like vandalism.
card.truth: A low fire is what keeps a sequoia grove alive. It burns up the dead wood on the ground before that wood can feed a big fire, the tree's bark is thick enough to shrug it off, and the heat opens the tree's cones so its seeds fall onto the bare soil they need.
steps: Dead branches, needles and logs pile up on the ground under the trees, year after year: fuel waiting for a fire.
A crew lights a low fire on a calm, damp day, and it creeps along the ground eating that fuel.
The flames reach the trunk and do little: a sequoia's bark is fibrous and up to 18 inches (46 cm) thick, so it resists burning and keeps the heat out of the living wood.
Hot air rises into the branches and dries out the old cones, which have held their seeds shut for as long as 20 years. They open, and within a week or two the seeds begin to fall.
The seeds land on soil the fire has swept bare, the only ground where they can sprout, with sunlight reaching it.
When a wildfire comes later, it reaches the burned ground and finds little left to burn: in 2021 one was stopped below the General Sherman Tree by a patch burned on purpose in 2019.
card.turn: For about a hundred years people put the fires out, and the fuel kept piling up. Then one wildfire in 2020 killed an estimated 7,500 to 10,600 large sequoias. A study in 2026 of about 26,400 sequoias in those fires found that trees standing where crews had burned on purpose were nearly four times more likely to survive.
card.ending: Blackened ground under the giant, its trunk scorched at the foot and green at the top, and a scatter of tiny green seedlings coming up through the ash. Said: putting every fire out is what nearly killed them. Lighting small ones is how they're kept alive.
card.inside: A cut through the trunk at ground level: flame against the bark, a heat glow that fades out inside the thick bark and never reaches the pale living wood. Then up in the branches: warm air as rising balls reaching a closed green cone, the cone drying brown and opening, seeds spinning down. Then from above: a wall of wildfire running through thick fuel, reaching the black burned patch and dying down.

a firefighter with a hand torch, standing
forest floor litter: needles, branches, logs
low ground flames and blackened ground
a cutaway of bark and wood at the trunk's foot
heat as a glow, warm air as rising balls
a sequoia cone, closed and open, with seeds

Still done today: NPS news release of 16 Oct 2026, a 482-acre prescribed fire in the Grant Grove area of Kings Canyon to start 17 Oct 2026 ('Prescribed burns promote the regeneration of giant sequoias'): https://www.nps.gov/seki/learn/news/update-prescribed-burning-planned-at-grant-grove-starting-october-17-to-reduce-wildfire-risk.htm ; and NPS, 24 Jun 2025, about 126 acres burned at Big Stump East to help defend Grant Grove. entries.idea: How one Chinese army grew from 40,000 men to a million while the other fought Japan's big battles
their_words: the chinese 40k into 1 million one

card.topic: How one Chinese army grew from 40,000 men to a million while the other fought Japan's big battles
card.hook: This army entered a war with 40,000 men. It left with a million.
card.first_picture: A war-room map table of China, 1937. Along the coast and the big rivers, a tall stack of blue blocks stands face to face with a line of white blocks marked with a red disc. Far off in the dry hills of the north-west sits one small red block, alone. A hand lifts a blue block off the table.
card.ending: The table in 1949: red blocks across the mainland, and what is left of the blue stack on the island of Taiwan. Said: 'Taiwan's government says that army used the war to build its strength. Beijing says its guerrillas were the backbone of the fight. What both governments' records agree on: one army fought the big set-piece battles, and the other fought as guerrillas behind the lines and was still growing when they ended.'
card.war: The war between China and Japan, 1937 to 1945, and the Chinese civil war that followed, 1946 to 1949. Three armies: Japan's, the Nationalist government's under Chiang Kai-shek, and the Communist Party's under Mao Zedong.
card.problem: Fight an invader with an army too small and too poorly armed to meet it in open battle, and still be standing when the war ends. In Mao's words of 1938: 'this large and weak country is being attacked by a small and strong country'.
steps: In 1937 Japan's army comes down the coast and up the rivers. The Nationalist government's army, the blue blocks, meets it in the big battles and is pushed back with heavy loss, year after year.

The Communist army is small: just over 40,000 men, by its own count. In May 1938 Mao writes its plan down: Japan 'does not have sufficient soldiers and has to leave many gaps in the occupied areas'. So go into the gaps behind its lines and build bases there: guerrilla units 'must preserve themselves and, moreover, they must expand', and his next sentence speaks of 'preserving and expanding ourselves and destroying the enemy'.
Japan holds the cities and the railways. In the countryside between them the red blocks fight a guerrilla war, raid by raid, and spread. How much that cost Japan is what the two sides still dispute.

In August 1940 that army fights its one big offensive in the open: the Hundred Regiments Offensive, 105 regiments against the railways of the north. Japan's answer falls hard on the base areas, and nothing on that scale is tried again.

In 1944 Japan sends about half a million men against the Nationalist armies, the largest land operation it ever ran. The blue stack loses hundreds of thousands more, and the red moves into the country left open behind.
1945: Japan surrenders. The blue stack is worn down and the red one is about a million. Four years of civil war later the red blocks hold the mainland, and the Nationalist government is on Taiwan.
card.how_known: What is documented, and what is a reading. Documented: who fought the big battles. Taiwan's government counts '22 major battles, over 1,000 large-scale campaigns, and over 38,000 smaller engagements' fought by the Nationalist government's forces (President Ma Ying-jeou, 29 Aug 2015, Office of the President, read), and that government's own tables give 1,319,958 killed, 1,761,335 wounded and 130,116 missing (Hsu Long-hsuen, as cited on Wikipedia, not opened; Ma's speech says over 3.22 million 'lost their lives'). Wikipedia's article on the war says the Nationalists were 'the main combatants opposing the Japanese in each of the 22 major battles' and, in a sentence that carries a footnote, that Communist forces 'usually avoided pitched battles with the Japanese, in which their guerrilla tactics were less effective, and generally limited their combat to guerrilla actions', with the Hundred Regiments Offensive and Pingxingguan as 'notable exceptions'. Beijing's own statement agrees on who fought at the front: Hu Jintao's speech of 3 September 2005 says 'As the main force on frontal battlefields, the KMT army organized a series of major campaigns... which dealt heavy blows to the Japanese army', and the same speech says the CPC waged 'extensive guerrilla warfare' in the rear and 'became the mainstay' (found and read by the fact-check, not by me: https://www.mfa.gov.cn/eng/xw/zyjh/202405/t20240530_11339773.html). Documented: the plan. Mao Zedong, 'Problems of Strategy in Guerrilla War Against Japan', May 1938 (Selected Works, volume II, read at marxists.org), quoted in the steps. Documented, by the Party's own count: the growth, from 'just over 40,000 men' in 1937 to 'a great army of one million' by 1945 (the editors' note to that text; Wikipedia's table has 1.2 million for 1945). Because the hook's two numbers are the Party's own, the second line heard says 'by its own count'. The readings. Taiwan's government holds that Mao's communists 'only used the war to strengthen their own forces': those words are Reuters' paraphrase of its position, not a quotation of an official. Beijing's position is that communist guerrillas were the 'backbone' of the fighting in China, again in Reuters' words. Both are from Reuters, 5 Sep 2025, read as carried by The Standard. Among historians, Rana Mitter's China's War with Japan (2013; Forgotten Ally in America), as two reviewers give it: 'While the communists were quite effective in guerrilla warfare', 'Mao preferred to keep his forces in reserve for the post-war battle for supremacy in China' (Sir Hugh Cortazzi, Japan Society review, read); 'the Communist side fought exactly one major battle against the Japanese, and a number of limited guerrilla actions.' (Jonathan Mirsky, The Spectator, 20 June 2013, read). Those are reviewers' words about the book, which I did not open. Cortazzi adds a sentence of his own, not Mitter's: 'The war enabled the Chinese Communist Party to seize power and destroy the Chinese Nationalists'. Pulling the other way, Hans van de Ven is cited on Wikipedia's article on Operation Ichi-Go (his books not opened) for the view that Japan's 1944 offensive, about 500,000 men, did damage to the Nationalists that shaped the post-war order: that puts the weight on what Japan did to one army, more than on what the other army chose. Mao's own later words are on record: to Japanese visitors on 10 July 1964, that the Japanese Imperial Army 'has been a good instructor for us' (Mao Zedong sixiang wansui, 1969, as translated on Wikipedia's article on these remarks, which cites the Chinese collections; whether he meant it as dark humour is argued there). Left out on purpose: the line often quoted as Mao's, '70 percent for self development, 20 percent for compromise, and 10 percent against Japan'. Wikipedia carries it with a 'citation needed' tag and I found no document for it. The owner's word 'hiding' is one side's reading and the card doesn't use it: what the 1938 text orders is guerrilla war behind the lines, and whether that was the only way a small army could fight or a way of saving itself for the next war is exactly what's argued. The 1940 offensive is 105 regiments and about 200,000 troops on Wikipedia, in an article that carries a neutrality-dispute tag; other accounts say 400,000, so the card gives regiments only. That 'nothing on that scale is tried again' follows Mirsky's 'exactly one major battle' and Wikipedia's 'notable exceptions'. A claim seen only in a search summary: that Communist Party historians have called the Nationalists' role 'important' and their own the 'cornerstone'. Not opened: Mitter's and van de Ven's books, Yang Kuisong's work on the guerrilla war, Chalmers Johnson's Peasant Nationalism (1962), Lloyd Eastman's Seeds of Destruction, or any Japanese army record (a Japanese defence-institute paper on the fighting in north China was found but couldn't be read).
card.left_today: The argument itself, every year. On the war's 80th anniversary, in September 2025, Beijing called its guerrillas the 'backbone' of the fight and Taiwan's government answered that Mao's communists 'only used the war to strengthen their own forces' (both in Reuters' words, not quotations of officials). The two governments this story ends with still face each other across the Taiwan Strait, which makes this a live political quarrel as well as history.
card.shown_as: Blocks on a map. No battle is shown, no city, no civilians, nobody hurt: losses are blocks lifted off a table. No leader's face: Mao and Chiang Kai-shek are named, never drawn. Neither army is called brave or cowardly, the word 'hiding' isn't used, and the short says who holds each reading.
card.silent: A hand taking blocks off a tall blue stack at a front line, while far behind the enemy's line a single red block turns into a pile. It reads without words as one shrinking and one growing, but it is a map table, not a bizarre sight: the silent test passes only that far.
card.mistake: Armies shrink in wars. This one fights as guerrillas, away from the big battles, and comes out twenty-five times the size it went in.
card.stake: China, and the soldiers of both armies. The Nationalist government's own tables count over 3.2 million of its men killed, wounded or missing in the eight years.
card.seen: A hand taking blue blocks off the table battle after battle while the tall stack shortens; a red stain spreading through the spaces between the railway lines Japan holds, with small red raids flickering along those lines year after year; one big burst of red arrows at the railways in 1940, and no second one; the red stack growing to a million; then red arrows crossing the whole map.

card.source: Mao Tse-tung, 'Problems of Strategy in Guerrilla War Against Japan', May 1938, Selected Works of Mao Tse-tung, volume II, read at the Marxists Internet Archive: 'this large and weak country is being attacked by a small and strong country'; 'Japan is a small country, she does not have sufficient soldiers and has to leave many gaps in the occupied areas'; 'it will be impossible to sustain guerrilla warfare behind the enemy lines without base areas'; 'to confine the enemy invaders to a few strongholds, that is, to the big cities and along the main communication lines'; 'they must preserve themselves and, moreover, they must expand'; and the editors' note that the Eighth Route and New Fourth Armies grew from 'just over 40,000 men' in 1937 to 'a great army of one million' by 1945. Office of the President, Republic of China (Taiwan), 29 Aug 2015, President Ma at the Navy's exhibition for the 70th anniversary: '22 major battles, over 1,000 large-scale campaigns, and over 38,000 smaller engagements'; 'Over 3.22 million ROC troops, including 268 commanding officers, lost their lives': https://english.president.gov.tw/NEWS/4725 Reuters, 'Explainer: What is the battle over China's wartime history?', 5 Sep 2025, as carried by The Standard: https://www.thestandard.com.hk/china/article/310888/What-is-the-battle-over-Chinas-wartime-history Sir Hugh Cortazzi's review of Rana Mitter, China's War With Japan, 1937-1945 (Penguin), Japan Society: https://www.japansociety.org.uk/review?review=436 Jonathan Mirsky's review, The Spectator, 20 June 2013: https://spectator.com/article/china-s-war-with-japan-by-rana-mitter---review Wikipedia, 'Hundred Regiments Offensive' (20 August 1940 to 24 January 1941, Peng Dehuai, 105 regiments, the Shijiazhuang to Taiyuan railway, Japan's sweeps of the base areas after it), 'Operation Ichi-Go' (April to December 1944, about 500,000 men citing van de Ven; 'the largest military operation carried out in the history of the Japanese army', Hara Takeshi; Chinese casualties put at 500,000 to 600,000 in Hsiung and Levine; Communist guerrillas gaining ground in the countryside after it) and 'Mao Zedong thanking Japan controversy': read as guides to their sources, which were not opened. That the red 'moves into the country left open' in 1944 is from the Ichi-Go article. The colours are the card's own choice.

entries.idea: The owner's idea: why a fork sparks in the microwave, when its metal walls don't
their_words: go

card.topic: The owner's idea: why a fork sparks in the microwave, when its metal walls don't
card.hook: A fork sparks in the microwave. The metal walls around it don't.
card.first_picture: Inside a dark, running microwave lit by its lamp: a steel fork on a plate on the turning glass tray, small blue-white sparks snapping at the tips of its tines, their flicker reflected in the metal walls all round it.
card.people_think: Metal and microwaves don't mix: any metal at all, a fork or a spoon, bounces the waves about, sparks, and can wreck the microwave.
card.truth: It isn't metal as such: the oven itself is a metal box, and a clean, undamaged oven's walls bounce the waves all day without a spark. What matters is shape and place. The waves shove the loose electrons in any metal back and forth. On a big smooth surface they spread out thin; at sharp points, a fork's tines or the creases in crumpled foil, they crowd together until the air at the tip gives way in a spark. Metal close to a wall can spark across to it, and thin metal can overheat and burn. So the metal that's made to go in, the rack some microwaves come with, has no loose ends, is held off the walls by plastic supports, and is built for that one oven.
steps: The oven makes waves that push back and forth 2.45 billion times a second, and its metal walls bounce them round and round through the food.
Every push shoves the loose electrons in any metal one way, then back the other.
On the big, smooth walls those electrons spread out thin, so the walls just bounce the waves, without getting very hot and without a spark.

In a fork they crowd into the four sharp tips, until the push at each tip is strong enough to tear electrons out of the air itself (air gives way at about 30,000 volts across a centimetre), and the air lights up: a spark.

A smooth spoon has no tips, so it's far less likely to spark, though makers like Frigidaire and LG still say no metal at all. Crumple foil and every crease becomes a tip, so it crackles; the makers that allow foil say a small, new, smooth piece shaped to the food, over no more than a quarter of it.
Close to a wall, a spark can jump across to it, so the makers that allow some metal say keep it off the walls: Panasonic says at least an inch (2.5 cm).
card.turn: Thin metal does more than spark. A twist tie is too thin for that sloshing current, so it can overheat and burn, and a plate's gold line sparks: Sharp says gilded ware can be 'completely ruined in moments'. One maker's manual warns that a thin metal strip in a food tray 'can burn the floor of the oven or ignite a paper towel', and the US National Institutes of Health's fire marshal says metal 'can spark, damage the unit and lead to a fire'. So the moment you see a spark, switch it off: caught at once, Whirlpool says, it shouldn't damage the oven, though a long one can.
card.ending: The wire rack that came with the oven, two plates of food on it in the glow: rounded bars joined into closed loops with no loose ends, resting on its plastic supports, not touching the walls, and not one spark. Said: it wasn't the metal alone. It was the points, the thin bits, and the walls too close. So the one piece of metal that's made to go in, the rack that came with the oven, has no points, stands clear of the walls, and is built for that one oven. Your fork has points, and wasn't built for it.
card.inside: Close and dark inside the cavity: the waves as faint glowing bands bouncing between the metal walls, the metal's electrons as small bright balls sliding back and forth with each wave. On the wall and on the spoon they spread thin and stay dim. In the fork they bunch into the four tips, the tips glow brighter, and the air at each tip lights into a small blue-white spark. Crumpled foil with a bunch at every crease; a small smooth piece shaped over one end of the food, dim. A gap badge between foil and wall shrinking until a spark jumps it. A gold rim sparking along its line, and a paper towel beside a twist tie browning. Last, the rack: balls flowing evenly round its closed loops with no bunching, its plastic feet holding it off the wall, at a badge reading 'not touching'.
needs: a real kitchen microwave, close and dark: metal cavity, lamp, glass turntable, door with its window
a plate of food with a steel fork, and a smooth steel spoon
kitchen foil: one sheet crumpled into a ball, one small fresh piece shaped smoothly over the end of the food
a plate with a thin gold rim, and a twist tie on a paper towel
the oven's own wire rack: rounded bars in closed loops on four plastic supports, with two plates on it
waves as glowing bands; electrons as small moving balls
small blue-white sparks, and a warm glow for heat
badges: 2.45 billion a second, about 30,000 volts a centimetre, 1 inch (2.5 cm) to the wall
card.source: How metal behaves, from a physicist's own page: Louis Bloomfield (University of Virginia), How Everything Works, answer of 17 Jan 1997 (the source_url): 'a microwave pushes electrons back and forth through any metals it encounters'; the oven's metal walls 'simply reflect the microwaves without becoming very hot and without emitting any sparks'; 'Electrons are more likely to leave the end of a metal surface at a sharp point'; 'Most spoons are smooth enough that no sparks will occur'; 'a thin twist-tie or small bit of aluminum foil may well overheat and begin to burn'. Scientific American, Mark Fischetti with Bloomfield, 'How the Microwave Works', 1 Nov 2008 (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-the-microwave-works/): 'metal does not necessarily cause sparking inside a microwave', 'the cooking chamber walls are metal', 'Shape matters', 'A flat, round, metal platter will spread charge around it, preventing buildup', and 'sharper points, such as fork tines or the many tiny edges in aluminum foil, concentrate charge' to make 'corona discharge—a spark'. The walls: US FDA, Microwave Ovens (content current as of 12 Oct 2023): 'The microwaves reflect off the metal interior of the oven'; 'Generally, metal pans or aluminum foil should also not be used'; 'Some ovens should not be operated when empty'. The frequency: HyperPhysics (Georgia State University), 'Modern microwave ovens operate at the frequency 2,450 MHz', a wavelength of about 12 cm. The air: Troy Messina, Electromagnetics I (Berea College, on LibreTexts), section 5.21: 'about 3 MV/m for air'. Said per centimetre, as NPTEL's high-voltage lecture gives it: 'The value 31 kV/cm is applicable only for d = 1, that is for one cm gap at 760 Torr and 20°C', and 'For gaps of a few mm, the electric strength is much higher' (so not 'per millimetre'). That it roughly holds at the oven's 2.45 GHz and normal pressure is from Khodataev's 2009 abstract (a library record, not the paper), so the badge says 'about'. That the field at a tip grows strong enough to pass it is the physicists' account above, not a number anyone measured in a fork. Foil: Sub-Zero Wolf's support page, in words that match the USDA's (whose own page refused to open, so the USDA is seen only in search summaries): 'Use new, smooth foil only. Wrinkled foil can cause arcing (sparks)'; 'Shape the foil smoothly to the food so no edges stick out'; 'Do not place the foil closer than one inch from the oven walls'. The inch for any metal: Panasonic's support page, 'When using foil, skewers, racks or utensils made of metal in the oven during Microwave or Combination cooking', 'allow at least 2.5 cm (1") of space between the metal material and interior oven walls'; LG's LMV1831 manual, 'Never allow metal to touch walls or door'. GE's 'Metal Cavity' support page gives the jump to the wall: metal utensils can cause 'arcing from the metal object to the nearest grounded object which is usually a wall'. Other makers allow no metal but the rack: Frigidaire; LG's help page, 'DO NOT place aluminum or metal like items in the microwave', and that metal 'will cause sparking and damage the microwave'; Sharp (16 Jul 2019), 'The short answer is absolutely not', and even smooth foil can arc 'if microwaves encountered points or edges'. Sub-Zero Wolf, for foil: 'use small amounts', 'Cover no more than 1/4 of the food with foil'. Gold rims: Panasonic, 'Do not use metal containers or dishes with metallic trim during Microwave or Combination cooking'; Emerson's 1100W manual, 'METAL CONTAINERS or dishes with metallic rims should not be used. Arcing may occur.' LG: 'Bowls or plates with gold or silver lined patterns will begin to spark'; Sharp: 'Any gilded flatware or utensil can cause arcing and be completely ruined in moments'. Fire: Emerson's manual, of a thin strip of metal in some styrofoam trays, 'When microwaved, the metal can burn the floor of the oven or ignite a paper towel'; the NIH Fire Marshal, giving NFPA's 2023 Fire Prevention Week message: 'The metal can spark, damage the unit and lead to a fire', and 'If you have a fire in your microwave oven, unplug the unit and leave the door shut.' Damage, which is half true: Whirlpool's support page, 'Prolonged arcing can damage the oven and/or the utensil', 'If caught at once, arcing should not damage the oven', 'Aluminum foil and some metal can be used in the microwave oven'. The fear for the magnetron belongs mostly to an empty oven: Panasonic, 'Operating the oven empty for a short time will not damage the oven', but it can 'cause damage to the microwave's magnetron'; Whirlpool's patent US 8,530,807 (2013): 'strong reflection from the cavity typically occurs when the cavity is empty. Such reflection may deteriorate or even destroy the magnetron.' That a fork beside food seldom harms the magnetron is our reading of these, with a 2006 Fraunhofer IVV study done for the European Aluminium Foil Association, seen only on that association's page and in summaries (no damage to four ovens heating foil trays at full power; its PDFs no longer open). The rack: GE Appliances' support page on the Double Duty Shelf, its metal shelves 'present no danger of arcing if they are properly inserted' and 'should not touch the back wall of the oven'; Frigidaire's FAQ: 'The plastic spacers which hold the rack in place are engineered to keep it from arching against the microwave's sides'; its tines and outer edges 'are engineered to form a fully enclosed object', avoiding 'the open ends that lead to arching'; 'No other metal objects, including pans, utensils, etc. are approved for use inside a microwave'; Sharp's Simply Better Living (16 Jul 2019): 'the rack that came with the oven is specifically machined not to have edges', and it can't be moved to another oven; LG: 'Only use the rack that is supplied'; Whirlpool: 'Always remove the rack after 2-level cooking', and 'Using the provided accessory racks with microwave function can cause arcing or sparking. To avoid damage... do not allow the rack or pan to touch the inside cavity walls, ceiling, or floor'; GE: 'All microwave cavities are "tuned" to a specific size and configuration, as are the metal racks that come in some models'. Dirty or damaged cavity walls can arc too (Whirlpool names soil build-up; GE has a cavity-repair page), hence 'a clean, undamaged oven' in the truth. Still sold: P.C. Richard's listing for Frigidaire's GMOS1968AF over-the-range microwave includes a 'Metal Rack'. Metal containers sold for microwaves: LG's manual allows 'shallow foil trays (if tray is 3/4 inch deep and filled with food to absorb microwave energy)'. The spark's colour: Whirlpool, 'Arcing (a blue flash of light)'. Not found: anything on a butter knife in particular, so it's left out; any maker saying a spoon is fine (Panasonic allows metal utensils an inch from the walls, Frigidaire approves none), so the short shows a spoon staying quiet and never tells anyone to try it. A near title of his, not about metal: 'Microwaving Two Grapes Creates Plasma' (cjQBP0Sg7mo, 4 Nov 2026, about 6.0M views) opens on the same sight, sparks in a running microwave; its captions weren't read. None of his microwave shorts covers metal: from their captions, the mesh screen is about keeping the waves in, the plate and ice about water, the person and the Earth about being cooked.

card.silent: Sparks snapping at the tips of a fork's tines inside a running microwave: it looks like a fire about to start, in an oven everyone owns.
card.mistake: Someone has left a fork in a running microwave, the one thing everyone's told never to do, and it's sparking. A stranger would think it's about to catch fire or wreck the oven. And the box around it is metal too, and isn't sparking.
card.stake: A fire in your own kitchen, and the oven itself: thin metal can light a paper towel, and a long arc can damage the oven. No life is at risk, so the stake is softer than a bird's brain or chicks in a box.
